newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands join Belgian steel workers in jobs march.
newsitem.headline: Thousands join Belgian steel workers in jobs march.

text.p: Thousands of demonstrators from across Belgium joined workers of bankrupt Belgian steel firm Forges de Clabecq on Sunday in a mass protest against job losses, company closures and social injustice.

"The march is all about giving a voice back to the grass roots..., asking them to take up their position again, and to insist on being heard," Roberto D'Orazio, leader of the socialist FGTB trade union at Clabecq, told Belgian radio.

Belgian television estimated the number of marchers at up to 20,000 by 3 p.m. (0900 EST/1400 GMT), shortly after the start of the rally through the town of Tubize near Brussels where the troubled steelworks is based.

Trade union organisers had called on everyone from workers to the unemployed, students and pensioners to join in. Many arrived by coaches and Belgian railways laid on specially scheduled trains from several towns in the south of the country.
"I am a teacher -- I want a future in this country for my pupils," one woman said.

Supporters at the rally included some of the 2,000 workers at the privately owned Boel steel plant in La Louviere, south-west of the capital. They face 800 job losses under a plan to merge Boel with Dutch steel firm Hoogovens.

The protest builds on the momentum of a rally in Brussels last week attended by 15,000 public sector workers who are angry at government plans to reform labour laws and worried about pensions and privatisation.
Parents caught up in Belgium's pedophile and murder scandal also came on Sunday to give their backing.

They led a "White March" in Brussels last October of 250,000 people who wanted to show their support for pedophile victims' families and to call for judicial reform. The parents say they are now concerned for the welfare of Clabecq workers' children.
"All these problems in Belgium are linked," said Gino Russo, a metalworker whose child was killed by pedophiles.

Clabecq -- which employs 1,800 -- was one of 768 Belgian companies to go bankrupt in January, a record 36-percent leap from the same month in 1996, according to figures from Belgian trade and company data group Infotrade.

Belgium's latest jobless figures put unemployment at 13.6 percent in December. The figure is calculated differently from European Union rates, which showed Belgian unemployment at 9.5 percent in November -- the most recent month available.
Since Clabecq was declared bankrupt on Jan. 3 liquidators have been trying to salvage the firm -- which has orders for the first quarter of 1997 -- and save most of the jobs at stake.

But Clabecq's majority shareholder and biggest creditor, Belgium's southern Walloon Region, last week turned down a request by the receivers for 800 million francs ($25 million) worth of financing, increasing doubt about the steelwork's future.
Saddled with high costs and low-grade products, the company had been struggling for months to survive in a cyclical, competitive industry weighed down by over-capacity.
Belgian banks are appealing a court ruling ordering them to extend credit lines worth 650 million Belgian francs ($20.4 million) to Clabecq for two months.

Clabecq filed for bankruptcy in mid-December after the European Commission rejected a 1.5 billion Belgian franc ($47 million) rescue plan by the Walloon Region, which then withdrew its suppport for the firm.
